claims.text: Al and Ti are low-density alloying elements, while Nb and Ta are refractory alloying elements.
The initial alloy is primarily BCC.
Rapid solidification produces a randomized atomic distribution with low inherent SRO in the proposed alloy.
Annealing near the order-disorder transition while remaining below the onset of long-range ordering or precipitation can induce controlled SRO.
Controlled SRO increases local lattice distortion.
Controlled SRO increases dislocation pinning and therefore mechanical strength.
Controlled SRO reduces oxygen diffusivity through the lattice.
Reduced oxygen diffusivity favors formation of a coherent, dense, adherent, self-healing oxide scale.
The proposed oxide scale improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Controlled SRO improves corrosion resistance.
A fully random atomic distribution has higher oxygen permeability and forms a less effective oxide scale.
A fully random atomic distribution has lower strength because it provides fewer local barriers to dislocation motion.
Relative to the random-state baseline, the SRO-treated alloy will have higher yield and tensile strengths.
Relative to the random-state baseline, the SRO-treated alloy will show slower oxidation kinetics and lower weight gain over time.
Relative to the random-state baseline, the SRO-treated alloy will exhibit improved corrosion resistance.
The SRO treatment will retain the alloy's low density.
Annealing beyond the SRO stability range can produce long-range ordering or precipitates.
Long-range ordering or precipitation can cause embrittlement and eliminate the proposed SRO benefits.
Service above the protective oxide's stability range will degrade oxidation resistance.
The magnitude of the joint strength and oxidation benefit and the optimal thermal-treatment window are not yet quantified.

contradictions.description: Long-range ordering, precipitation, and oxide instability are defined as conditions outside the hypothesis's intended validity range, but the falsification rule also treats deleterious ordering or oxide spallation as falsifying outcomes. Such outcomes could instead show that the treatment or test left the stated domain, rather than refuting the within-domain SRO mechanism.
